narrative:
Your application was denied because the model estimated an 82.7% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That does not mean failure is certain; it means the information reviewed placed you in a high-risk group, and the school chose not to admit you on that basis.

The strongest reason was your third-year class standing. You were recorded in the lowest decile, while accepted students averaged around the sixth decile. This was the most influential factor and pushed the prediction toward likely bar failure. Your first-year class standing was the second most important factor: you were also in the lowest decile there, again well below the accepted-student average, and it added further weight toward failure. Your LSAT score was the third most important factor. A score of 28 is below the accepted-student average of about 37, and it also pushed the prediction toward failure.

To improve your position, ask admissions whether you can discuss the decision or appeal, and provide any context the numbers do not capture. Focus on a concrete bar-readiness plan: address the academic weaknesses reflected in your class standing, consider retaking the LSAT if feasible, and seek advising or preparatory support. If you reapply, show evidence of improvement and a realistic plan for passing the bar.
